summary: Details IETF policies on rights in Contributions, designed so that contributions can be made available to the IETF and Internet communities while letting authors keep as many rights as possible. It was replaced by RFC 5378.

eli5.summary: When you add a drawing to a group project, this sets the rules for who may copy it and what you still own. A newer rulebook replaced it.

questions: what rights do ietf authors grant
subtitle: The 2005 rules for what rights people give the IETF when they submit a draft, and what they keep.

tldr.problem: The exact meaning of the copyright and rights rules in Section 10 of RFC 2026 had been debated for years, leaving unclear what contributors grant to the IETF.
tldr.mechanism: By submitting a Contribution, the author grants ISOC and the IETF a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide license for publishing, translation and (usually) derivative works within the IETF process, makes some representations, and the document carries standard notices.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3978 was replaced by RFC 5378 and was also updated by RFC 4748, so it is no longer the current statement of the policy.

facts.label: Draft lifetime
facts.value: 6 months nominal in the public directory

today: RFC 3978 is no longer current: it was obsoleted by RFC 5378 and was also updated by RFC 4748. It had replaced RFC 3667 and, with RFC 3979, replaced Section 10 of RFC 2026.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
Under the laws of most countries and treaties such as the Berne Convention, authors get rights in their work automatically, and an employer often receives them when the work is done on the job. For works to be used in the IETF Standards Process or published as Internet-Drafts, limited rights in every Contribution must be granted to the IETF and the Internet Society (ISOC). This memo (BCP 78) spells out those rights and the representations that go with them.

It exists because the intent of Section 10 of RFC 2026 had been the subject of vigorous debate. The aim is to clear up ambiguities, not to substantially change current policy. A companion document, RFC 3979, covers rights in the technology itself, such as patents. The memo says it is not legal advice.

Key terms come first. An IETF Contribution is any submission meant to become part or all of an Internet-Draft or RFC, plus statements made within an IETF activity, including spoken ones in IETF sessions and messages to working group or IETF mailing lists. An RFC Editor Contribution is a draft meant for the RFC Editor as an Informational or Experimental RFC, outside the IETF Standards Process.
sections.eli5: Anything you share with the group counts, even something you say out loud at a meeting. The memo first explains who and what the rules cover.

sections.title: Rights Granted in IETF Contributions
sections.content:
When someone submits a Contribution, that person and each named co-Contributor are deemed to agree to the terms, on behalf of any organization they represent. They grant ISOC and the IETF a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide license under all intellectual property rights in the Contribution to copy, publish, display and distribute it in the IETF Standards Process or in an Internet-Draft, to prepare or allow translations, and to make derivative works within the IETF Standards Process unless the notices in the Contribution forbid it.

The license also lets the IETF reproduce trademarks included in the Contribution, and lets anyone extract and reuse executable code or code fragments in an IETF Document (such as MIB modules) for any purpose. That code license does not grant any patent rights. The Contributor also lets the IETF and ISOC reference the contributor's name and address.

The Contributor represents, to the best of their knowledge and ability, that major contributors are acknowledged, nothing in it is confidential, nothing limits the ability to grant these rights that is reasonably and personally known to them, and nothing was intentionally included that is defamatory, untrue or illegal. No confidential material may be submitted, and any confidentiality statement in a Contribution can be disregarded. The IETF has no duty to publish a Contribution, and may withdraw one that does not comply.
sections.eli5: When you give the group your drawing, you let them copy it, translate it and update it for their own work, and you promise it is really yours to give. You still own it.

sections.title: Required Notices in Documents
sections.content:
Every IETF Document must carry certain notices, reproduced verbatim, including in copies, derivative works and translations. Internet-Drafts must include an IPR Disclosure Acknowledgement stating that applicable patent claims have been or will be disclosed under Section 6 of BCP 79. All IETF Documents carry a copyright notice saying the document is subject to the rights, licenses and restrictions in BCP 78 and that, except as set forth there, the authors retain all their rights, followed by an AS IS disclaimer of warranties.

The copyright notice does not mean ISOC owns the contribution itself. It signals that ISOC claims rights in aspects such as layout, the RFC numbering convention and the prefatory language, while the contribution stays with its authors or in the public domain.

Authors who do not want the IETF to make derivative works can add one of two limitation notices, and authors who want only an Internet-Draft can add the line This document may only be posted in an Internet-Draft. These limits may not be used on standards-track documents or with most working group documents, since the IETF must keep change control. A working group may discuss such a draft, but the author must resubmit it without the limits before the group formally adopts it. An abbreviated notice is allowed for extracted material such as MIB modules. RFC Editor Contributions follow a lighter regime of their own (Section 4 and Section 6).
sections.eli5: Every shared page gets the same stamp at the end saying whose rules it follows. If you want only to show a page and not let others change it, you can write that on it, but the group may then not use it for its own work.

sections.title: Why the Rules Look This Way
sections.content:
The stated goal is to obtain from authors only the non-exclusive rights needed to develop and publish IETF Documents, and leave all other rights with the authors, who cannot withdraw the granted rights. The derivative-works right matters because the IETF has to evolve its documents in response to deployment experience and changing conditions, so it is required for standards-track documents and most others. Translation rights are required before anything can be published as an RFC.

There are two exceptions: documents that describe proprietary technologies, whose owners may not want the IETF to produce a revised version and call it the new version, and republications of the work of other standards organizations. Rights granted cover individuals taking part in the IETF, but do not extend broadly to their employers or sponsors.

Section 8 adds that documents not subject to copyright, such as those produced by the U.S. government or in the public domain, are still asked for the same grants and representations, to the extent they may be protected.
sections.eli5: The group only asks for the bits of permission it truly needs, so it can print, translate and improve its own papers. Everything else stays with the author.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says it relates to IETF process, not any particular technology. It notes there are security considerations when adopting any technology, but there are no known issues of security with the IETF Contribution rights policies.
sections.eli5: This is a rulebook about sharing, not about a gadget that could break, so the authors found no safety problems to warn about.
